​An incredible premise that feels completely squandered. I wanted to see how a freak event could slowly fracture a perfect marriage and reveal entirely new flaws in both of them. Instead, the movie shows its hand too early: the guy is already a selfish mess, so the avalanche doesn't actually trigger anything new. The final act is just baffling. The logic completely breaks down : why are they skiing in dangerous conditions, and why is she going along with it? Are we seriously supposed to root for this guy's 'redemption' arc because he 'saves' her after crying like a toddler while admitting to cheating and lying? Even during the final bus scene, she’s the one taking charge anyway. By the time they’re all just walking down the road at the end, the movie has completely lost the plot. That being said, the movie does have its redeeming factors. The acting across the board is great, and there are some genuinely fantastic, beautifully shot scenes. (With the notable exception of that random night scene with the drone flying against the mountains, which looks incredibly fake and CGI-heavy.)

A pretty clear example of what happens when you have a interesting concept but with bad execution. Aside from this playing like a stereotype of everything that's made fun of by Scandinavian movies, I just don't care about the couple. When the event took place and the man ran off, I was excited. But then he's hopeless because he can't own what he did, and she's hopeless because she says she's fine, but then dumps all their trauma in the lap of another couple with no warning to either him or the couple. The movie wants to use this fight as a commentary on not only the couple but to have a bigger conversation about masculinity, how easily it can turn fragile and how that fragile masculinity can look like. But no only do I have 0 care for the relationship, I think the movie fails with the commentary too. Since he can't own up to it, so we don't ever get into the core of the issue, when the third act comes along and the movie is about to wrap up and people start crying because strong emotional "breakthroughs" are happening, I'm left rolling my eyes. When a movie really tries to say something deep and it fails, to me that's the definition of pretentious. This isn't the most pretentious movie I've seen, but it definitely is on the list. The couple is so loveless and bland that when the Hivju and Metelius enters the story, I immediately got more interested in their dynamic, but by that point it's a bit too late. Then there's also the conversation about being able to be married and hooking up with someone else on the side which also goes nowhere. There's just way too much going on here and it's not going anywhere. It's also a bit annoying to see another "romantically-inclined" movie from Scandinavia that portrays love like this. So emotionless and cold. Maybe there's no wonder there's less marriages and hooking up going on these days compared to before. I'm sure the shallow dating apps aren't helping, but these couples are the only ones we're seeing these days, and they're depressing as fuck. I'm watching this as prep for a story I have a few months to write. Going into it I feared I was going to see stuff that would make it pointless for me to write my story, as it was going to talk about similar themes, but finishing this, I feel it's all close to untouched still. Good for me, bad for this story.

A single moment of crisis shatters the image of proactive, protective masculinity Tomas and his family have constructed around him. Force Majeure employs a clinical, alienating aesthetic of minimalist compositions that drain the Alpine resort of any warmth or coziness. The pristine white snow and hotel interiors are like a sterile laboratory. Every lingering frame feels hollow. And at the end of it all, after the denial, the gaslighting, the breakdown... Tomas, having experienced no real growth beyond earning the pity of his children, is offered a foggy 'rescue' scene that feels entirely staged. His wife Ebba allows him to play the proactive protector so he can reclaim the image of his so-called masculinity and their children can reclaim a sense of normalcy. This is his heroic moment, right? He's a 'man' again, right? Wrong. The film immediately undercuts this false redemption in the bus scene, where Ebba is once again the proactive one. She alone confronts the erratic driver who can't handle the controls of his own vehicle, and she alone gets him to open the doors so everyone can exit to safety, while Tomas sits passively. But, this time, he's willing to admit a fault to a member of his family instead of denying it to the point of breaking everything and everyone around him. Yes, he does smoke. Yes, he has lied. No, he's not picture perfect. Maybe there's some small amount of hope for him yet.

Force Majeure really got to me. I kept thinking about how one instinctive moment can completely change the way you see someone you thought you knew. It’s also a smart take on masculinity and the pressure to always be the strong, protective one. The silences are excruciating, the awkwardness is borderline funny, and at times it genuinely felt like I was watching a real family go through this rather than watching a film.

I guess I should have started with Force Majeure instead of Triangle of Sadness if I wanted to discover Ruben Östlund, because this is exactly the kind of satire I've been waiting for. I was expecting a film about loss, or about how a family must survive after an avalanche, but the reality was even better. The avalanche is really just the beginning: Force Majeure is much more interested in how a family can survive a marriage after one person's reaction exposes something that everyone would rather not see. And Östlund makes that uncomfortable situation genuinely hilarious. I loved just how cringe and painfully funny this can be, with more than one scene that made me want to yell at the characters for their horrible behaviour and reactions. The film constantly puts its characters in situations where there is no good way to save face, and then simply lets the awkwardness sit there. Conversations become increasingly uncomfortable as Tomas (Johannes Bah Kuhnke) tries to deal with what he did, while Ebba (Lisa Loven Kongsli) refuses to let him simply move past it. The highlight for me is the scene with the couples discussing what happened. It's such a great example of what Östlund does best: taking an incredibly awkward social situation and turning it into something both hilarious and genuinely thought-provoking. The discussion isn't simply about whether Tomas was right or wrong to run away. It's about how we imagine ourselves behaving in a crisis, how we expect men and women to behave, and what happens when our instincts don't match the person we believe ourselves to be. That's what makes the film so effective. Östlund doesn't need to turn Tomas into a monster, or Ebba into a perfect victim. He simply keeps pushing these people into situations where their ideas about themselves start falling apart. The comedy comes from watching them desperately try to reconstruct those ideas. Maybe the ending wasn't exactly what I was expecting—or what I wanted it to be. It feels slightly off compared with what Östlund had been presenting to us from beginning to end, and I'm still not entirely convinced by the direction it takes. But even with that reservation, Force Majeure is an incredibly sharp and uncomfortable piece of satire, and exactly the kind of film I was hoping to find after Triangle of Sadness . This is the quality I expected from Östlund's later works: painfully funny, deeply uncomfortable, and very good at making you question what you would actually do when the moment comes. Best of the 2010s

10/10 Ruben Östlund’s “Force Majeure” is a darkly comic Swedish film that examines masculinity, family, and the human desire to maintain control in the face of danger. Set almost entirely within a luxurious ski resort in the French Alps, the film follows Tomas (Johannes Bah Kuhnke), his wife Ebba (Lisa Loven Kongsli), and their two children, Vera (Clara Wettergren) and Harry (Vincent Wettergren), during what is supposed to be a relaxing family holiday. However, when an apparently controlled avalanche suddenly threatens the family, Tomas makes a split-second decision that exposes a deep contradiction between the man he believes himself to be and the man he actually is. Through awkward silences, uncomfortable humour and carefully constructed compositions, Östlund explores how quickly social expectations can collapse when people are confronted with fear. The central event of the film is the controlled avalanche that approaches the restaurant where Tomas and his family are eating. Although the avalanche is eventually revealed to have been stopped safely, Tomas’s reaction is deeply damaging to his family. Rather than protecting his wife and children, he instinctively runs away, taking his phone with him while Ebba remains with the children. This moment is deliberately presented without melodramatic music or conventional action-film heroics. Instead, Östlund allows the audience to observe Tomas’s behaviour almost clinically. The comedy comes from the gap between the seriousness with which Tomas regards his role as a father and husband and the embarrassing reality of his actions. The avalanche therefore becomes more than a physical threat. It acts as a metaphor for the sudden collapse of Tomas’s carefully constructed identity. Before the incident, he presents himself as a successful, responsible family man. He is concerned with his work, his children and his position within the family. Yet when confronted with genuine danger, this identity proves fragile. His instinct is not to behave according to the heroic masculine ideal that he appears to value, but to save himself. Östlund uses this contradiction to question whether masculinity is an authentic quality or a performance sustained by social expectations. Ebba’s response to Tomas is equally important. Initially, she seems more disturbed by his behaviour than he is himself. She repeatedly brings up the incident, forcing Tomas to confront what happened. His discomfort is heightened by the fact that he cannot easily explain his actions. He attempts to minimise the situation, but Ebba refuses to allow him to dismiss it. Their relationship consequently becomes a struggle over memory, responsibility and truth. Tomas wants the event to become insignificant; Ebba wants it acknowledged. The more he tries to control the narrative, the more unstable his position becomes. Östlund’s use of humour is particularly effective because the situations are rarely funny in themselves. Instead, the humour emerges from social discomfort. Characters often say too much, remain silent for too long, or behave in ways that reveal anxieties they would rather conceal. The audience is placed in the uncomfortable position of watching private tensions become public. This style allows Östlund to criticise social conventions without turning the film into a straightforward moral lesson. We are encouraged to laugh at Tomas, but we are also forced to recognise the uncomfortable possibility that fear might make hypocrites of any of us. The film also examines the way masculinity is constructed through the expectations of other people. Tomas’s crisis is not simply that he failed to protect his family; it is that he believes this failure has made him less of a man. His shame becomes increasingly visible as the film progresses. He is desperate to restore the image of himself as courageous and dependable. This culminates in an exaggerated emotional breakdown in front of his family, in which he appears to confess and accept responsibility. The scene is both pathetic and strangely sincere. Tomas is performing vulnerability, but that does not necessarily make the emotion false. Östlund suggests that masculinity can become so bound up with performance that even genuine emotion is difficult to separate from theatrical behaviour. The character of Ebba provides an important counterpoint to Tomas. She is not simply a victim of his failure but someone who is also fascinated by the social implications of the incident. Her own behaviour becomes increasingly complicated, particularly when she discusses the event with other people. Östlund avoids presenting either partner as entirely rational or morally superior. Instead, both characters are shown as people attempting to construct versions of themselves that they can live with. The film’s humour comes partly from exposing the distance between these self-images and their actual behaviour. The ski resort itself contributes significantly to the film’s themes. Its vast white landscapes are beautiful but also strangely impersonal. The snow creates an environment in which people appear small and vulnerable, while the controlled explosions used to prevent avalanches suggest an attempt to impose order upon nature. This mirrors the characters’ attempts to control their own lives and identities. The resort promises safety, luxury and predictability, yet the possibility of catastrophe is always present. In this sense, the setting reinforces one of the film’s central ideas: human beings like to believe that they are in control, but that control can disappear in an instant. Östlund’s visual style strengthens this sense of artificial order. Many scenes are composed with precise, symmetrical framing, making the characters appear almost trapped within the architecture around them. The clean lines of the hotel contrast with the chaotic emotions taking place inside it. Long, static shots often prevent the audience from escaping an awkward situation through rapid editing. Instead, we are made to sit with the characters’ discomfort. This creates a distinctive form of comedy in which embarrassment becomes almost unbearable. The film’s title is therefore significant. A force majeure is an extraordinary event that prevents someone from fulfilling an obligation, and the avalanche initially appears to offer Tomas a convenient explanation for his behaviour. Yet the film complicates this idea. The avalanche may have created the circumstances, but it did not completely determine Tomas’s response. His instinctive decision reveals something about him that he would rather not acknowledge. The real crisis is therefore not the avalanche itself but the discovery that his understanding of himself may have been false. Ultimately, “Force Majeure” is a film about what happens when people are forced to confront the difference between who they think they are and who they actually are. Through Tomas and Ebba’s increasingly strained relationship, Östlund explores masculinity, parenthood, shame and the social pressure to appear competent and courageous. His use of dark comedy prevents the film from becoming sentimental, while its restrained visual style makes the characters’ emotional discomfort even more powerful. The avalanche lasts only a few moments, but its consequences dominate the rest of the film. In that sense, Östlund suggests that the most frightening disasters are not necessarily those that threaten our physical safety, but those that destroy the stories we tell ourselves about who we are.
